html:
The Aqua Appia was the first aqueduct of Rome, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, the same man who built the Appian Way.

It brought water from springs east of the city, about 16 km away, and ran almost entirely underground. That kept the water cool and clean, and it also hid the channel from enemies at a time when Rome was fighting the Samnite Wars. It entered the city near the Porta Capena and ended near the cattle market by the Tiber, a crowded part of town.

The springs were found by Appius's fellow censor, Gaius Plautius, but the aqueduct was named after Appius alone. He stayed in office past the usual term to finish his projects, a sign of how unusual his career was.

The Appia began one of Rome's great engineering traditions. Later came the Anio Vetus in 272 BCE and the Aqua Marcia in the 140s BCE, the first to run on high arches. By the end of the 1st century BCE the Appia had fallen out of use as an aqueduct; see Roman aqueducts.
sum: The Aqua Appia was the first aqueduct of Rome, begun in 312 BCE by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, the same man who built the Appian Way.
